Contusion

/kun-TOO-zhun/ - the stress falls on TOO · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Contusion means a bruise caused by a blow.

A contusion the size of a plum bloomed where the cabinet door had caught her forearm.

Worked Example

Falling off a horse looks dramatic; the visit that follows is mostly about ruling things out. Rosa's arm swelled where it had struck the rail, and by evening the mark had gone a deep violet. The scan showed the bone whole, and the skin had never opened — a contusion, the doctor said: crushed capillaries bleeding quietly under intact skin, six ugly days of color and nothing worse.

Contusion is the exact word for what Rosa took away, because a contusion is a bruise caused by a blow — the clinical name for blood let loose under skin that held. A gash opens the surface; a break reaches the bone; a contusion stains the middle layer and heals from the inside.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bruise: Bruise is the everyday, kitchen-table word for the mark a blow leaves — blood let loose under skin that held. A contusion is the same injury in chart language: the clinical term the report uses when precision matters. You show a friend the bruise; the radiologist writes contusion.

shiner: A shiner is slang for one particular bruise — the black eye, and only the black eye. A contusion can bloom anywhere a blow lands: forearm, hip, shin. Around the eye, described over the kitchen table, a contusion turns into a shiner; everywhere else it keeps the clinical name.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

healing: the mark's slow undoing

soundness: tissue whole and unmarked

Where it sits · how deep the injury goes — scrape → contusion → break

scrape vs. contusion: A scrape is far milder than a contusion — it takes the skin's top layer and is forgotten inside a week, while a contusion bleeds quietly under skin that held.

break vs. contusion: A break goes further than a contusion — a contusion bleeds quietly under skin that held; a break reaches the bone beneath it.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: thoroughly (an intensifier)

Root — tus

Root — tus: pounded (Latin tundere)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: the result of

Put it together

Put it together: Con- (thoroughly) + tus- (pounded) + -ion (the result of) = the result of a thorough pounding. Latin tundere meant to beat or to bruise; a contusion is what the beating leaves behind, written in Latin and shown in purple.

Why there's no fresh relative to spot

Why there's no fresh relative to spot: Latin tundere, 'to pound,' left almost nothing else behind in English. Its one common survivor is obtuse — an angle or a mind pounded blunt — which this course teaches on its own card, so contusion has no new relative to hand you here. Remember the pounding instead: a contusion is the mark it leaves.

Strength Check

Word Choice

clinical / formal

Contusion is chart language: precise, unsqueamish, a bruise with paperwork. Say bruise at the kitchen table; say contusion when the scan comes back clean and the report needs the exact word for blood under unbroken skin.
